place.zh: 外门演武场 · 五行台
place.en: The outer court training ground · the Five Elements Platform

setup.zh: 你站在台边，把那只手翻过来，低头看着自己的掌心。
setup.en: You stand at the edge of the platform, turn that hand over, and look down at your palm.

recap.zh: 你的掌心烙下一个印子：一个圈，圈里一横，搓不掉。决赛，九层的「祁不退」祁长松一招进一步，你的法术、痒痒针全叫他的护体灵光弹开，一步一步把你压到台边；香只剩一指，他出了掌，你挨住了，把猪蜻蜓拍在他背上——风掉头，两个人一齐飞起来，撞了两棵老柏；他撕了符，落在起脚处后头三尺——二十年头一回退了一步；你的腰带挂在西角的柏树上。「……祁长松，胜。」筑基丹归了他；观主对你说：「前四，进内门名册。」
recap.en: A mark was branded in your palm: a circle with a bar across it, and it won't rub off. In the final Qi Changsong, layer nine, Never-Back Qi, came on one step a move; his guarding light threw off every spell and needle you had, and step by step he pressed you to the edge; with one finger of incense left he struck, you took the palm and slapped the pig-copter on his back — the wind turned, the two of you flew up together and banged off both old cypresses; he tore the charm and landed three feet behind where he'd stepped from — his first step back in twenty years; and your belt hung you over a branch of the west cypress. "…Qi Changsong wins." The Foundation pill went to him; the abbot told you: "The last four go into the inner register."

zh: 掌心正中，烙着一个印子。
en: In the middle of the palm, a brand.
A circle, with a bar across it.
"…You caught it with a mirror. The hand caught it anyway."

story.zh:
小满站起身来，把那只手翻过来，低头看着自己的掌心。

掌心正中，烙着一个印子。不红，不肿，是一道一道发白的细线，像是从肉里头长出来的：一个圈，圈里一横。

他拿拇指去搓，搓不掉；拿指甲去刮，刮得皮都红了，那个圈，那一横，还在那里，白白的，凉凉的。

一个很低的声音在他耳朵里道：「……你拿镜子接了。」小满小声道：「嗯。」那声音道：「手还是挨了。」隔了很久，才又道：「……傻子。」便没有声息了。

褚先生站在人群最后头，一只手捋着山羊胡子，捋到一半，停在半空。隔了好一会儿，才有一个声音怯生生地道：「……他……他那是……反噬了吧？」这一声给众人打开了一扇门：「对对对，反噬！镜子照人，照到他自己脸上去了！」「一夜吞了三瓶丹，灵力是虚的，压不住那面镜子，光倒打回来了！」「褚先生讲过的，轻则退三层，重则废！」「我就说他脸上那些斑不对劲——你看，全烙白了！」越说越信，越信越觉得自己早就看出来了。褚先生的山羊胡子终于落了下来，他咳了一声，沉着脸道：「丹药之道，贪多必失。诸位引以为戒。」说罢转身走了，走的时候，回头看了小满一眼，看的是他垂在身边的那只手。台角的执事这才想起手里的锣，敲了一下：「马小宝不能再打了。沈小满，胜。」

当时谁也没去想，一面缺了角的破铜，怎么接得住那一镜。褚先生之外，还有两个人没跟着说反噬。一个是台北面竹椅上的观主玄沉子，他从头到尾没动过，这时候却轻轻「嗯」了一声。另一个是山门台阶上的瞿老，他背对着演武场，一直在扫地；镜子裂开的那一声，他的扫帚停了，停在半道上。那三百级台阶，他扫了五十年，这一天，没有扫完。
story.en:
Xiaoman stood up, turned his hand over, and looked down at his palm.

In the middle of the palm a mark was branded. Not red, not swollen: fine white lines, as if they had grown out of the flesh — a circle, with a bar across it.

He rubbed it with his thumb and it didn't rub off; he scraped it with a nail till the skin went red, and the circle, the bar, were still there, white, cold.

A very low voice said in his ear: "…You caught it with a mirror." "Mm," he whispered. The voice said: "The hand caught it anyway." A long while later: "…Fool." And then nothing.

At the very back, Master Chu stood with a hand on his goatee, stopped halfway down. After a long while a timid voice said: "…He… that was… backlash, wasn't it?" That opened a door: "Yes, yes, backlash! The mirror shone on him — straight back into his own face!" "Three bottles in one night — his power's hollow, he couldn't hold the mirror, the light came back on him!" "Master Chu told us — at best you drop three layers, at worst you're crippled!" "I knew those blotches weren't right — look, they've all burned white!" The more they said it the more they believed it, and the more they believed it the surer they were they'd seen it all along. Master Chu's goatee finally came down. He coughed, and said sternly: "In the way of pills, greed brings loss. Take warning, all of you." He turned to go, and going, looked back once at Xiaoman — at the hand hanging at his side. Only then did the steward at the corner remember the gong in his hand, and struck it once: "Ma Xiaobao can't go on. Shen Xiaoman wins."

At the time, nobody stopped to wonder how a chipped scrap of bronze had caught that flash. Besides Master Chu, two others didn't join in the talk of backlash. One was the abbot Xuanchenzi in the bamboo chair north of the stage; he hadn't moved the whole time, but now he gave a soft "Mm." The other was Old Qu on the gate steps, his back to the training ground, sweeping all along; at the sound of the mirror cracking his broom stopped, stopped halfway. That stair of three hundred steps he had swept for fifty years; that day, he never finished it.

label.zh: 攥着拳上台：决赛，对祁长松
label.en: Up with your fist hidden: the final, against Qi Changsong

exits.means: the final against Qi Changsong, layer nine, who will not touch him: spells eaten by his earth shield, the palm taken at the last finger of incense, the pig-copter slapped on his back, both flown into the cypresses — he lands on one foot at the edge and wins; no pill

story.zh:
日头挨着西边山尖的时候，另一个半边也打完了。内门那个七层把一套掌法在祁长松身上打了三遍，打得满头大汗，自己认了输。

决赛，沈小满对祁长松。

小满上台的时候，右手攥着拳，藏在袖子里，左臂上那圈新布条又洇出了一点红。祁长松已经站在了台对面。他四十来岁，脸是方的，一双眼睛半睁半闭，看了一眼小满的袖子，道：「马师弟那一镜，你接了。」小满道：「他自己照干了。」祁长松道：「我不伤你。我送你下去。」说完，眼皮一垂，再不说话。香点着了。

我送你下去——台下的人都当是瞧不起。阿禾那张纸上写的是：没法打，认输。她看的是底册，小满看的是脚。他看了他一上午的脚。祁长松一步迈出去，脚底下的青石板便沉一沉；一掌推出来，推的不是一只手，是那一步踩着的整块地。前脚踩实了，后脚才跟上来——后脚跟上来的那一霎，是他身上最轻的时候，比眨一下眼还短，二十年，没有人抓住过。

可知道是一回事，打得过是另一回事。祁长松迈了第一步。小满先扔法术：两只手里扣着的一颗火弹、一根冰锥，一样一样打过去；他往后退，退一步，掐一诀，又是一道金刃。祁长松身上浮着一层土黄的光，薄薄的，像缸上的一层釉，火弹、冰锥、金刃撞上去，「当」「当」「当」，石子打在缸上一般，弹了开去。小满又掐一诀，扔木藤——木吃土——藤尖在那层光上扎出一个白点，便软了。祁长松又迈了一步。小满一咬牙，袖子里那三根痒痒针一齐扬了出去。三根针碰着九层的护体灵光，「叮」「叮」「叮」，弹得满天乱飞：一根扎进了青石板缝里，一根不知飞到了哪里，第三根拐了个弯，飞进台下人堆，正扎在一个内门师兄的腮帮子上。那师兄「嗯？」了一声，拿手一摸，嘴角一抽，「嘻」；又一抽，「嘻嘻」；跟着便捂着肚子弯下了腰：「哈哈哈——我没想笑——哈哈哈哈——」笑得眼泪直流，旁边的人扶都扶不住。祁长松又迈了一步。

他一步一掌，不快，不急。小满躲得开头一掌，躲不开第三掌；躲得开掌，躲不开那一步——那一步迈上来，台上便少一块地方。他往左绕，祁长松往左迈；他往右绕，祁长松往右迈，像一面山坡，一寸一寸往前挪。小满上去推他，推不动；退开三步一头撞上去，像撞在一堵墙上，自己弹回来，摔在青石板上，左臂的伤口迸开了，血洒了一地。他爬起来，又给一掌推出去三尺；再爬起来，又三尺。五掌下来，他鼻子里、嘴里都是血，脚后跟底下，青石板只剩了半寸。祁长松从头到尾，没往后挪过一寸。

台下起先还笑：「四层的，下来吧，别耽误人家吃晚饭！」笑到后来，没人笑了。有人喊：「别撞了！」又有人喊：「撞他！」喊着喊着，喊「撞他」的越来越多。香，烧过一半了。

小满站在台边喘气，从怀里摸出一个油纸包，抽出一张黄纸来。台下的人伸长了脖子：一只猪，背上两对翅膀。「符？」「四层的人画的符？」「画的是猪？」祁长松那双半睁半闭的眼睛，睁开了。他的神识从那张纸上扫过去，扫了个空——一丝灵气也没有；可这个孩子捧着它，像捧着一件宝贝，这个孩子方才接裂了一面镜子。他最怕的，就是神识读不出来的东西。他抬起来的那只脚，又放了回去。这张纸是做什么的，小满不知道，一回也没试过；那一夜他按着铜肚子念的是「给我一样打得过内门的」，他赌的就是这一句。他把那张纸攥在手心里，舔湿了背面。

他攥着那张猪，等着。他爹说过，日头落山那一下，山里的风要掉个头——白天往山上走，夜里往山下走；掉头的那一下，林子里的鹿都要抬头。

香只剩一指的时候，日头沉下去了。演武场边上那面旗先是一垂，小满便动了。他不绕，不躲，从台边上直直地朝祁长松走过去，像一个打昏了头、只晓得往前走的孩子，那张黄纸攥在手里，朝前伸着。

祁长松的眉头，头一回皱了起来。二十年。他在内门往前走了二十年，没退过一步，等这一颗丹等了二十年，香只剩一指了，这个浑身是血的四层，捏着一张他读不透的纸，自己往他跟前走；台下两百多人，喊的全是「撞他」。那张纸不能沾身。他的手，在袖子里动了一动。

祁长松出掌了。

小满看见了。他等的，就是这一掌。那一掌印上来之前，他怕得脚底发凉；印上来的那一霎，心里反倒静了，静得像蹲在雪地里等鹿。

那一掌不快，也不响，只是推了出来，平平地印在小满胸口上。大比不许伤人性命，这一掌量好了的：推得倒一个四层，推不死。可它落下来的那一霎，台下有人尖叫起来——小满整个人往后一折，一口血喷了出来，喷了祁长松一袖子。

他没有倒。

他的脚在青石板上往后犁出去半尺，脚底下那块地，却像生了根——秘境里那一撮土，在他丹田里长成的那一块厚地，存得住水，也挨得住这一掌。他晃着，弓着，就是没有倒，两只手往前一捞，一把揪住了祁长松的袍子，像一个挨了打、站不稳的孩子去抓旁边的大人。

祁长松这一掌推出去，人跟着迈了一步，前脚踩得青石板一沉；脚底下那股土气，跟着那一掌，全走到了手上。他后头那只脚，正要跟上来——这一霎，是他二十年来最轻的一霎。

小满揪着他袍子的那只手，往他背上一拍。那张猪蜻蜓，贴在了祁长松的后背上。

便在这时，演武场边上那面旗「哗」地翻了个面。风掉头了。

祁长松两只脚，离了地。

台下「啊」的一声，两百来张嘴一齐张开了。祁不退，在内门往前走了二十年、没退过一步的祁不退，给一张画着猪的黄纸提了起来，一寸，两寸，脚尖离了青石板。他到底是九层，身子一飘起来，一只手已闪电般反抓过来，一把揪住了小满的后领——要走，一块儿走。

两个人一齐飘了起来。

飘得并不好看。祁长松那张二十年没变过颜色的方脸，绿了又白，白了又绿；他头朝前，屁股朝后，一只手揪着小满，一只手往背上去够那张符；小满给他揪着领子，两条腿在半空里乱蹬，像一只叫人拎着后颈的猫。那猪蜻蜓专往树上撞，认准了演武场东角那棵老柏，一头撞了过去，「咚」的一声，弹回来；又认准了西角那棵，「咚」的一声，又弹回来。台下的人抱着脑袋四下乱躲，方才挨了一针、这时候还在「嘻嘻」的那个内门师兄，躲得慢了，发髻叫小满一脚踢歪了，他捂着脑袋在原地转了三圈，一面笑一面叫：「我的头！哈哈——我的头！」祁长松在半空里打了个转，总算够着了背上那张黄纸，「嘶」的一声，撕成了两半。

他撒了小满的领子，自己往下一落，落在了五行台的边上——不是他起脚的地方，是那地方后头三尺。一只脚的脚尖点着石沿，脚跟悬在外头，身子晃了一晃，又晃了一晃，袍袖张开像一只落枝的鹤，到底站住了。

小满没有落下来。西角那棵老柏的一根横杈，从他肚子底下兜了过去，勾住了他的腰带。他对折着挂在杈上，脑袋垂在这一边，两条腿垂在那一边，两只胳膊也耷拉着，晃荡着，像一件搭在晾衣绳上的湿袄子，鼻子里的血一滴一滴，往下滴。

便在这时，执事敲响了铜锣。那半炷香，到了。

执事看看台边上脚跟悬空的那一个，又看看树上挂着的那一个，锣槌在手里转了两转，才道：「……祁长松，胜。」

那一声落下去，全场翻了天——一半是笑，「哈哈哈哈」，笑得前仰后合，笑得有人坐在地上捶腿，有人笑岔了气，一声接一声地打嗝；一半是吼，吼的是「祁不退退了！」「退了一步！」「二十年，头一回！」笑声和吼声搅在一处，滚过五行台，滚过四棵老柏，滚得山门那边的鸟都飞了起来。

小满挂在树上，倒着看这一场。输了。他心里先是一空，一口气提了一整天，这时候泄了，泄得他连手指头都抬不起来。挂了一会儿，血往脑门上涌，他忽然觉得这样子实在好笑——一个四层，打了一天，打到最后，挂在树上，像他娘晾的一条咸鱼。他倒挂着，「噗」地笑出了声，跟着便「哈哈哈」地收不住了，一笑，肋下那根骨头一疼，又笑，又疼，笑得在树杈上一晃一晃，真像一条叫风吹着打秋千的咸鱼。

祁长松站在台边，一身的汗，袖子上是小满的血。他低头看了看自己的脚后跟，又抬眼看了看三尺开外、他起脚的那块青石板，看了很久，才抬起头，看着树上挂着的那个孩子，道：「二十年。头一回退了一步。」又道：「你那张符，哪来的？」小满在树上晃了一晃，倒着答：「……捡的。」祁长松看着他，没说信，也没说不信，冲他点了一点头，走下了台，走的时候，伸手把那个发髻歪了、还在「嘻嘻」的师兄扶了一把。
story.en:
When the sun touched the western peaks, the other half was done too. The inner-court layer seven went through a whole set of palm strikes on Qi Changsong three times over, till the sweat poured off him, and yielded.

The final: Shen Xiaoman against Qi Changsong.

When Xiaoman went up, his right hand was a fist, hidden in his sleeve, and the fresh cloth on his left arm was already blotting red again. Qi Changsong already stood across the stage. He was about forty, square-faced, his eyes half open, half shut. He glanced at Xiaoman's sleeve. "Brother Ma's mirror — you caught it." "He shone himself dry." "I won't hurt you," said Qi Changsong. "I'll see you off the stage." And he lowered his eyelids and said no more. The incense was lit.

I'll see you off — everyone below took it for contempt. A He's page had said: can't be fought, concede. She had read the records; Xiaoman had read the feet. He had watched those feet all morning. When Qi Changsong stepped, the bluestone under his foot sank a little; when his palm went out, what it pushed was not one hand but the whole piece of ground that step stood on. The front foot set down solid, and only then did the back foot follow — and the instant the back foot followed was the lightest he ever was, shorter than a blink, and in twenty years no one had caught it.

But knowing was one thing; beating him was another. Qi Changsong took his first step. Xiaoman threw spells first: the fire bolt and the ice spike held ready in his two hands, one after the other; then he gave ground, a step back, a sign pinched, and a metal blade. Over Qi Changsong lay a film of earth-yellow light, thin as the glaze on a vat, and fire, ice and metal struck it — *clang, clang, clang* — like pebbles on a vat, and glanced off. Xiaoman pinched another sign and threw a wood vine — wood eats earth — and the vine's tip pricked one white dot on that light and went limp. Qi Changsong took another step. Xiaoman set his teeth and flung the three tickle needles from his sleeve all at once. Three needles against a layer nine's guarding light — *ting, ting, ting* — they glanced off and went flying every which way: one stuck in a crack of the bluestone, one went who knows where, and the third swerved off into the crowd and stuck in the cheek of an inner-court senior. "Hm?" he said, and put a hand to it; the corner of his mouth twitched — "Hee"; twitched again — "Hee hee"; and then he was doubled over clutching his stomach: "Hahaha — I'm not trying to laugh — hahahaha —" laughing till the tears ran, and the men beside him couldn't hold him up. Qi Changsong took another step.

One step, one palm, not fast, not hurried. Xiaoman could dodge the first palm, not the third; could dodge the palm, not the step — every step that came on, the stage was one piece smaller. He circled left, Qi Changsong stepped left; he circled right, Qi Changsong stepped right, like a hillside moving forward an inch at a time. Xiaoman went in and pushed him: he didn't budge. He backed off three paces and rammed him headfirst: like hitting a wall; he bounced back and fell on the bluestone, and the wound in his left arm burst open and spattered blood over the stone. He got up and a palm pushed him three feet back; got up again — three feet more. After five palms there was blood in his nose and his mouth, and under his heels there was half an inch of bluestone left. From first to last Qi Changsong never moved an inch backward.

Below, they laughed at first: "Layer four, get down, don't keep the man from his supper!" After a while nobody laughed. Someone shouted: "Stop ramming!" Someone else: "Ram him!" And as they shouted, more and more were shouting "Ram him!" The incense was past half.

Xiaoman stood panting at the edge, took an oilpaper packet from his coat, and drew out a sheet of yellow paper. The crowd craned: a pig, with two pairs of wings on its back. "A charm?" "A charm drawn by a layer four?" "Is that a pig?" Qi Changsong's half-shut eyes opened. His spirit sense swept the paper and met nothing — not a wisp of spirit power; yet the boy held it like a treasure, and the boy had just cracked a mirror. What he feared most was the thing his spirit sense couldn't read. The foot he had lifted went back down. What the paper did, Xiaoman didn't know; he had never once tried it. That night, with his hands on the bronze belly, he had asked for something that could beat the inner court — that was the whole of his bet. He held the paper in his palm and licked its back wet.

He held the pig and waited. His father had said: the moment the sun goes behind the hill, the mountain wind turns round — by day it climbs, by night it runs downhill; and the moment it turns, every deer in the wood lifts its head.

With one finger of incense left, the sun went down. The banner at the edge of the training ground first sagged, and Xiaoman moved. He didn't circle, didn't dodge; he walked from the edge straight at Qi Changsong, like a child beaten senseless who only knows to keep walking forward, the yellow paper in his fist, held out in front.

For the first time Qi Changsong's brow knitted. Twenty years. Twenty years he had gone forward in the inner court and never stepped back, twenty years he had waited for this pill, there was one finger of incense left, and this blood-soaked layer four, holding a paper he couldn't read, was walking up to him of his own accord; two hundred-odd below were all shouting "Ram him!" That paper must not touch him. His hand moved in his sleeve.

Qi Changsong struck.

Xiaoman saw it. This palm was what he'd been waiting for. Before it landed he was so afraid his soles went cold; the instant it landed, he went still inside, still as crouching in the snow waiting for a deer.

The palm was neither fast nor loud; it simply pushed out and pressed flat on Xiaoman's chest. No taking a life in the contest, and this palm was measured: enough to knock down a layer four, not enough to kill. But the instant it landed, someone below screamed — Xiaoman folded backward and a mouthful of blood sprayed out, all over Qi Changsong's sleeve.

He didn't fall.

His feet ploughed half a foot back across the bluestone, but the ground under them seemed to have taken root — the pinch of earth from the hidden realm, grown in his dantian into a thick piece of land, could hold water, and could take this palm too. He swayed, bent double, and did not fall; his two hands scooped forward and seized a fistful of Qi Changsong's robe, like a beaten child who can't stand grabbing the grown-up beside him.

As Qi Changsong's palm went out he stepped in with it, his front foot sinking the bluestone; the earth power under his feet went with the palm, all of it, into his hand. His back foot was just coming after — and that instant was the lightest he had been in twenty years.

The hand that held his robe gave his back a slap. The pig-copter was stuck to Qi Changsong's back.

At that moment the banner at the edge of the training ground flapped — whap — and turned over. The wind had turned.

Qi Changsong's feet left the ground.

Below, an "Ah!" — two hundred-odd mouths opening at once. Never-Back Qi, who had gone forward twenty years in the inner court without one step back, was being lifted by a yellow paper with a pig drawn on it, one inch, two inches, his toes leaving the bluestone. He was layer nine after all; as his body floated up, one hand snapped back like lightning and seized Xiaoman by the back of the collar — if he was going, they'd go together.

The two of them floated up together.

Not prettily. Qi Changsong's square face, which hadn't changed colour in twenty years, went green then white, white then green; he went head first, backside after, one hand gripping Xiaoman, the other groping at his back for the charm; Xiaoman, held by the collar, pedalled his legs in the air like a cat picked up by the scruff. The pig-copter went for trees and nothing else: it fixed on the old cypress at the east corner and rammed straight into it — thunk — and bounced back; fixed on the one at the west corner — thunk — and bounced back again. Below, people ducked and scattered with their arms over their heads; the inner-court senior who had taken the needle, still giggling, was too slow, had his topknot kicked crooked by Xiaoman, clutched his head, spun three times on the spot, and yelled between giggles: "My head! Haha — my head!" Qi Changsong turned a circle in midair, got hold at last of the yellow paper on his back, and — rip — tore it in two.

He let go of Xiaoman's collar and dropped, landing on the edge of the platform — not where he had stepped off from, but three feet behind it. The toe of one foot on the stone rim, the heel hanging out over nothing, he swayed once, and again, his sleeves spread like a crane alighting on a branch, and kept his footing.

Xiaoman didn't come down. A branch of the old cypress at the west corner swung in under his belly and caught his belt. He hung folded over it, head dangling on one side, legs dangling on the other, arms hanging limp, swinging, like a wet jacket thrown over a washing line, blood dripping from his nose drop by drop.

At that moment the steward struck the gong. The half stick was done.

The steward looked at the one at the edge with his heel over nothing, then at the one hanging in the tree, turned the gong-stick twice in his hand, and said: "…Qi Changsong wins."

The words fell, and the whole place erupted — half of it laughter — "Hahahaha!" — people doubled over, people sitting on the ground pounding their legs, people laughing so hard they got the hiccups, one hiccup after another; half of it roaring: "Never-Back Qi went back!" "He took a step back!" "Twenty years, and the first time!" Laughter and roaring churned together, rolled over the Five Elements Platform, over the four old cypresses, till the birds over by the gate took off.

Xiaoman hung in the tree and watched it all upside down. Lost. First a hollow — a breath held all day, let out now, so he couldn't lift a finger. After hanging a while, with the blood rushing to his head, it suddenly struck him as too funny — a layer four, fighting all day, ending up hanging in a tree like a salted fish his mother had hung out to dry. Upside down, he burst out laughing, and then the "Hahaha!" wouldn't stop; laughing hurt the rib, and he laughed again, and it hurt again, laughing till he swung back and forth on the branch, for all the world a salted fish swinging in the wind.

Qi Changsong stood at the edge, drenched in sweat, Xiaoman's blood on his sleeve. He looked down at his own heel, then up at the bluestone three feet off where he had stepped from, looked a long time, and only then raised his head to the child hanging in the tree. "Twenty years," he said. "The first time I've gone back a step." Then: "That charm of yours — where did it come from?" Xiaoman swung a little in the tree and answered upside down: "…Found it." Qi Changsong looked at him, said neither that he believed it nor that he didn't, gave him one nod, and walked down off the stage, and on the way he put out a hand and steadied the senior with the crooked topknot, who was still giggling.
